Adverse events & patient-safety incidents

  • Adverse event: a healthcare-related incident that results in patient harm or worsening of condition — including post-operative complications.
  • Near miss: an incident with potential for unacceptable consequences that does not cause harm, only because of chance or timely prevention.
  • Near miss = an incident that could have caused unacceptable consequences but did not occur. 439
  • Patient-safety complications may come from human, communication, system, environmental, medication, or procedural factors.
Inadequate communication between healthcare staff is one of the most common causes of adverse events / complications.

Causes of adverse events

Communication & handover

  • Inadequate communication between junior/senior staff, multidisciplinary teams, patients and families is a major source of error.
  • Proper endorsement/handover is essential: the patient's condition, ongoing problems, management, and required follow-up.
  • Poor coordination during handovers → loss of continuity and serious complications.
  • Never leave a patient without clear clinical responsibility/coverage.
  • Communicate openly with the patient and make sure they understand their condition.
  • Seek colleagues' opinions when uncertain; intra-operative assistants may spot findings the primary surgeon misses.
  • Rule of thumb: early communication + early escalation/change of plan can prevent deterioration.

Human & staffing factors

  • Psychological/cognitive overload increases error risk.
  • Inadequate staffing or insufficient knowledge, clinical skills, operative skills or experience compromises safety.
  • Clinicians doing unfamiliar procedures/technology need training and supervision (e.g. an inexperienced operator using advanced laparoscopic techniques).
  • Healthcare workers must understand the hospital's systems, resources and procedures.
  • Example of a human factor: error in the use of investigations (staffing levels, similar drugs and new technology are counted under other factor groups in this question). 437
  • Same question in the final: human factor → error in doing an investigation. 437 Final

System / organizational factors

  • Lack of clear procedures/protocols.
  • Inadequate staff coordination, supervision or training.
  • Cost/resource policies may influence patient care.
  • Hospitals need an incident-reporting system; patient-safety incidents should be reported.
  • Warning: if the institution lacks the capacity, expertise, facilities or equipment → escalate to administration and arrange referral/transfer.

Environment & resources

  • Safety is affected by environment, infrastructure and facility design. Risks include lack of: appropriate facilities, equipment/instruments, basic supplies (e.g. gloves), skilled expertise.
  • The ER and operating room are complex, high-risk environments where errors can have serious consequences.

Medical & technological complexity

  • Increasing medical complexity and new/advanced technology increase risk when personnel lack experience. Medication interactions/adverse effects may also contribute.
  • Laparoscopy with no CO₂ left — never insufflate oxygen (it supports combustion) or other gases: "Sorry, it is not safe." 435

Medication safety

  • A medication order should clearly state:
ElementWhy it matters
DrugExact agent being ordered/given
DosePrevents under/overdosing
IndicationConfirms the clinical rationale
DurationPrevents unnecessarily long/short therapy
RouteCorrect method of delivery
  • Danger: similar or related drugs create prescribing/allergy risks. Penicillin/cephalosporin cross-allergy ≈ 15% (as stated in the lecture).
  • Warning: parenteral/infusion errors can be dangerous — always verify drug, dose, route, concentration and administration (example discussed: an adrenaline infusion error).
  • Patient died from a medication interaction → first action as a provider: root cause analysis (find the system cause, don't punish individuals). 429 Final ×2

Hazard classification (from past exams)

  • The hazard class that deals with radiation, laser, furniture, floors, buildings and storage → keyed physical (physiological in one version) hazard. 429 Final 429 Final
  • Other classes: environmental, ergonomic (posture, lifting, repetitive work), safety & disaster codes (fire, evacuation codes).

Blood transfusion safety

Blood transfusion is a particularly high-risk process. Transfusion errors can cause severe complications and may be fatal.
  • Before transfusion, strictly confirm patient identity (ID/name and blood-related identification details).
  • Monitor the patient during transfusion, including pulse/vital signs.

Informed consent & communication

  • Core principle: consent is a communication process, not merely signing a form. A signed form is never a substitute for adequate discussion.
DomainWhat the patient must understand
DiagnosisDiagnosis or possible diagnosis, and current condition
PurposeGoals of treatment or surgery
ProcedureDetails/nature of the planned procedure
RisksMaterial risks/possible complications
BenefitsExpected benefits
AlternativesOther options, with advantages/disadvantages of each
OperatorWho is responsible for performing the operation [q:cfea3d0f435]
  • The responsible surgeon/operator should obtain consent for the procedure they will perform.
  • Explain risks in an understandable, balanced way rather than frightening the patient.
  • Do not present uncertain diagnoses or outcomes as definite (a suspected malignancy is explained as a possibility, not as confirmed/cured).
  • Discuss reasonable alternatives even when less effective — e.g. liver tumors: radiofrequency ablation and microwave ablation.
  • Key rule: the patient may change their mind / withdraw consent at any time before the procedure. Patients remember how complications and discussions were handled.
  • A competent adult signs his own consent — his son cannot sign for him. 437 ×2
  • Life-threatening emergency, nobody available → no consent needed (implied consent). 442 441 438 ×2

WHO surgical safety checklist (from past exams)

StepWhenWhat is done
Sign inBefore induction of anesthesiaConfirm patient identity, site, procedure, consent; site marked?; anesthesia & pulse-oximeter check; allergies; airway; blood-loss risk [q:eda7ab33435] [q:99c9bfe2437]
Time outBefore skin incisionTeam introduce themselves; confirm patient, site, procedure; anticipated critical events; antibiotic prophylaxis given; imaging displayed
Sign outBefore the patient leaves the ORNurse confirms the procedure performed; "all instruments and sponges are out" (counts); specimen labelling; equipment problems [q:d16e0636439] [q:95095ea1437]
  • Wrong knee listed, site not yet marked → time-out/verification with the team and the patient, then mark the correct site. 442
  • Universal precautions: never re-sheath needles — discard sharps directly in a sharps container. 438

Professionalism & surgical competence

  • Core competencies: knowledge, clinical skills, operative/technical skills, clinical experience, decision-making, communication, medical ethics & professionalism.
PhaseDecision-making focus
Pre-operativePlanning, work-up and consent decisions
Intra-operativeReal-time judgement as findings evolve
Post-operativeMonitoring, escalation and follow-up
  • When circumstances change: recognize the problem, communicate it, seek opinions, and modify management early.

Teamwork in the OR

  • Encourage communication rather than silencing junior staff/assistants — others may recognize anatomy, complications or technical problems from a different viewpoint. Speaking up prevents operative errors.

Patient assessment & professional conduct

  • Build rapport: sit with the patient, take a proper history, examine, and attend to their concerns.
  • Structured history + examination + relevant investigations before management.
  • Do not rely on tests while neglecting examination (e.g. abdominal pathology needs inspection for distension and hernia).
  • Examine female patients with a nurse/chaperone when required; keep dignity, consent and professionalism.

Operative / procedural safety

  • Follow the correct steps of the procedure; don't operate without a structured technique.
  • Avoid aggressive tissue handling — excessive force → tissue injury, bleeding and excessive adhesions. Use controlled, patient, gentle handling.
  • Prepare properly before operating.
  • Sources of procedural error: poor preparation, misinterpretation of findings, incorrect technique, misuse of surgical instruments.
Preventing complications = communication + staffing/training + supervision + resources + accurate medication/transfusion practice + informed consent + sound judgement + professionalism + teamwork + careful technique.

Mastery checklist (from the notes)

  • Communication failure is the most common cause of adverse events — handover always includes condition, problems, plan and follow-up.
  • Adverse event (harm occurred) vs near miss (harm avoided by chance/timely action).
  • Transfusion = top high-risk process: confirm identity and monitor vitals.
  • Medication orders: drug, dose, indication, duration, route; watch penicillin/cephalosporin cross-allergy (~15%).
  • Consent = communication, never just a form; the responsible operator obtains it.
  • Never present an uncertain diagnosis as definite; always disclose alternatives.
  • Patients can withdraw consent any time before the procedure.
  • Gentle tissue handling prevents injury, bleeding and adhesions.
